triage.name: Central retinal artery occlusion
triage.reason: Sudden painless monocular vision loss with a cherry-red spot; a stroke-like emergency reachable by history, fundoscopy and workup.

auto-repaired: workup: 'Optical coherence tomography of the macula' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if diagnosis uncertain on fundoscopy)
auto-repaired: workup: 'CT angiogram of head and neck' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if carotid duplex nondiagnostic or dissection suspected)
auto-repaired: workup: 'Transesophageal echocardiogram' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if TTE nondiagnostic and high suspicion for cardiac source)

exam: term 'Cherry red spot at macula' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Retinal arteriolar narrowing' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Most common in older adults, with a mean onset in the 60s
Men are slightly more affected than women

risk_factors.text: Recent myocardial infarction or valvular heart disease

chief_complaints.text: I suddenly can't see out of my right eye
Everything went black in one eye

hpi.onset: Sudden, over seconds; many notice on awakening
hpi.duration: Vision loss is maximal at onset; patients usually present within hours
hpi.progression: Abrupt and maximal at onset; there is little or no progression. Some patients report brief episodes of transient monocular blindness before the event.
hpi.quality: Painless severe dimming, gray-out, or complete blackness of vision
hpi.severity: Severe; often only finger counting or light perception remains
hpi.timing: Sudden, often while at rest or on waking

associated_symptoms.text: Brief episodes of vision loss in one eye before the event
Jaw pain brought on by chewing
Tenderness over the scalp or temples

pertinent_negatives: Focal weakness, numbness, or speech difficulty

positives.text: Sudden loss of vision in one eye
Prior brief loss of vision in one eye that fully recovered

argues_against: Sudden painful red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma
Chest pain or severe dyspnea may point to an alternative acute cardiovascular event
Weakness or speech difficulty suggests hemispheric stroke

atypical.how_it_differs: In patients over 50, especially women, giant cell arteritis may be the cause; headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or proximal muscle aches may accompany the vision loss.
Rare; may occur with congenital heart disease or hypercoagulable states. Young children may not report monocular vision loss and instead appear visually inattentive or bump into things.
missing_classic_features: Clear report of sudden painless vision loss in one eye

general.mild: Alert, comfortable, and may not appear systemically ill; the only complaint is monocular vision loss.
general.moderate: Alert, anxious about the vision loss, but appears otherwise well.
general.severe: Alert and anxious; may need help navigating due to severe monocular visual loss, but no systemic distress.
general.critical: Alert; may be distressed or unable to see well enough to ambulate safely, but no shock or respiratory compromise.

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity in each eye with a Snellen chart or near card; if too poor, test finger counting or hand motion.
findings.finding: Markedly reduced visual acuity in the affected eye, often only finger counting, hand motion, or light perception.
Pupil of the affected eye dilates paradoxically when light is swung from the unaffected to the affected eye.

findings.maneuver: Dilate the pupil and examine the fundus with a direct or indirect ophthalmoscope.
findings.finding: Cherry-red spot at the macula surrounded by pale, edematous retina.

findings.maneuver: Examine the retinal arterioles on fundoscopy.
findings.finding: Retinal arterioles are narrowed, sometimes with boxcar segmentation of the blood column.
No retinal tear or detachment; retina is attached.
No optic disc swelling or hyperemia; disc margins are sharp.

findings.maneuver: Palpate the temporal arteries and scalp.
findings.finding: Temporal arteries are nontender, non-nodular, with normal pulsation; no scalp tenderness.

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to hold both arms up and check for drift; test grip strength.
findings.finding: No arm drift or leg weakness.

findings.maneuver: Listen to spontaneous speech and ask the patient to repeat a phrase.
Ask the patient to name objects and repeat a sentence.

labs.caveat: Elevated in giant cell arteritis; normal in atherosclerotic or embolic CRAO. Do not delay steroids if GCA is suspected.
Elevated in giant cell arteritis; may be more sensitive than ESR.
Mild thrombocytosis can accompany giant cell arteritis.

findings.finding: Atrial fibrillation with irregularly irregular rhythm

imaging.preferred_when: First-line for evaluating carotid artery stenosis without radiation

findings.text: Hemodynamically significant internal carotid artery stenosis (≥70%)
Atherosclerotic plaque with irregular or ulcerated surface
Normal carotid arteries

imaging.preferred_when: Initial cardiac evaluation for embolic source

findings.text: Left atrial enlargement
Left ventricular thrombus
Valvular heart disease (e.g., aortic stenosis, mitral stenosis)
Normal study

imaging.preferred_when: When TTE is nondiagnostic and high suspicion for cardiac source

findings.text: Left atrial appendage thrombus
Aortic arch atheroma
Patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunt

imaging.study: Optical coherence tomography of the macula
imaging.preferred_when: When diagnosis uncertain or to assess retinal edema

findings.text: Inner retinal edema with increased thickness and hyperreflectivity
Loss of distinct inner retinal layer architecture
Delayed arteriovenous transit time
Absent or severely delayed arterial filling
Boxcarring of dye in retinal arterioles

imaging.preferred_when: When focal neurologic symptoms or concern for concurrent cerebral ischemia

findings.text: No acute cerebral infarction
Acute infarction in the ipsilateral cerebral hemisphere or borderzone

imaging.study: CT angiogram of head and neck
imaging.preferred_when: When carotid ultrasound nondiagnostic or dissection suspected

findings.text: Significant internal carotid artery stenosis or occlusion
Carotid artery dissection
No significant carotid stenosis

imaging.preferred_when: When giant cell arteritis is suspected

findings.text: Hypoechoic halo sign around temporal artery

initial.why: Detect atrial fibrillation as a cardioembolic source
Baseline platelets and hemoglobin; thrombocytosis may accompany giant cell arteritis
Screen for giant cell arteritis in patients over 50
Screen for giant cell arteritis; more rapidly responsive than ESR
Evaluate for ipsilateral carotid stenosis as embolic source
Evaluate for cardiac embolic source (thrombus, valve disease, atrial enlargement)

initial.only_if: focal neurologic symptoms or concern for embolic stroke

supporting.why: Assess and treat vascular risk factors
Screen for diabetes as a vascular risk factor

supporting.test: Optical coherence tomography of the macula
supporting.why: Confirm retinal edema when diagnosis uncertain

supporting.test: CT angiogram of head and neck
supporting.why: Further evaluate carotid or vertebral arteries
supporting.only_if: carotid duplex nondiagnostic or dissection suspected

supporting.why: Better visualize left atrial appendage and aortic arch
supporting.only_if: TTE nondiagnostic and high suspicion for cardiac source

supporting.why: Noninvasive evaluation for giant cell arteritis

supporting.only_if: young patient, no atherosclerosis, or recurrent events

not_indicated.why: No role in retinal artery occlusion
No role in isolated monocular vision loss

decision_points: Do not delay steroids if giant cell arteritis is strongly suspected; start immediately after ESR and CRP.
Admit as a stroke equivalent and obtain urgent vascular and cardiac evaluation.
Avoid ocular massage or other unproven acute interventions unless in a clinical trial.

differential.name: Giant cell arteritis
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless vision loss in an older adult can be caused by GCA, either as CRAO or arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy.
differential.trigger: Age over 50 with new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or proximal muscle pain

exam: Tender, nodular, or pulseless temporal artery
Pale swollen optic disc if anterior ischemic optic neuropathy rather than CRAO
imaging: Temporal artery ultrasound may show halo sign

differential.name: Retinal detachment
differential.why_considered: Sudden monocular vision loss with loss of visual field can mimic CRAO.
differential.trigger: Flashes and floaters or a curtain-like visual field loss

history: Progressive curtain or shadow across vision

differential.name: Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless unilateral vision loss in an older adult with vascular risk factors.

exam: Segmental optic disc edema with pallor
No retinal whitening or cherry-red spot

differential.name: Central retinal vein occlusion
differential.why_considered: Painless monocular vision loss with retinal findings.

history: Blurred vision rather than complete blackness

exam: No cherry-red spot or retinal whitening
imaging: Ocular ultrasound if no view to retina

differential.name: Optic neuritis
differential.why_considered: Acute monocular vision loss, especially in younger patients.

history: Subacute progression over hours to days
exam: No cherry-red spot or retinal whitening
imaging: MRI brain and orbits may show optic nerve enhancement

severity.mild: Unilateral vision loss with partial preservation of central acuity due to a cilioretinal artery; no systemic symptoms or signs of giant cell arteritis.
severity.moderate: Typical complete central retinal artery occlusion with severe monocular vision loss and classic cherry-red spot, but no signs of giant cell arteritis or urgent systemic emergency.
severity.severe: Complete central retinal artery occlusion with no light perception or with signs of giant cell arteritis such as jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or markedly elevated ESR or CRP.

red_flags.finding: Jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or temporal artery tenderness
red_flags.meaning: Giant cell arteritis; start steroids immediately to protect the fellow eye

red_flags.finding: Focal weakness, slurred speech, or facial droop
red_flags.meaning: Concurrent cerebral ischemia; treat as a stroke emergency
Carotid artery dissection; obtain urgent vascular imaging

red_flags.finding: Recurrent episodes of amaurosis fugax before the event
red_flags.meaning: Embolic source; urgent cardiac and vascular evaluation

red_flags.finding: Age over 50 with elevated ESR or CRP
red_flags.meaning: Giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise

complications.name: Permanent severe visual loss
clues: Vision remains finger counting or worse

special_populations.differences: Always evaluate for giant cell arteritis; check ESR and CRP and ask about jaw claudication or scalp tenderness.
Rare; suspect congenital heart disease, hypercoagulable state, or trauma. Young children may present with visual inattention rather than a clear complaint.

key_questions.question: When did your vision change, and how quickly did it happen?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden, painless monocular vision loss that is maximal at onset, often noticed on waking

key_questions.question: Are both eyes affected, or just one?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral involvement; bilateral simultaneous loss suggests another process

key_questions.question: How bad is the vision in the affected eye right now?
key_questions.looking_for: Severe loss, often only finger counting, hand motion, or light perception

key_questions.question: Before this happened, did you have brief spells of vision loss in the same eye that recovered?
key_questions.looking_for: Amaurosis fugax, suggesting an embolic source

key_questions.question: Do you have any pain in the eye or a new headache?
key_questions.looking_for: Absence of eye pain; new headache or jaw claudication raises concern for giant cell arteritis

key_questions.question: Are you seeing flashes, floaters, or a curtain or shadow over your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; flashes, floaters, or curtain suggest retinal detachment or vitreous hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or facial droop?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; focal neurologic symptoms suggest concurrent cerebral ischemia

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or an irregular heartbeat?
key_questions.looking_for: Atherosclerotic risk factors or atrial fibrillation as embolic sources

key_questions.question: Have you had any heart attacks, strokes, or procedures on your carotid arteries?
Have you had any recent scalp tenderness, jaw pain with chewing, or muscle aches?
key_questions.looking_for: Giant cell arteritis symptoms; requires immediate steroids

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or have you ever smoked?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco use as a vascular risk factor

key_questions.question: Do you take any blood thinners such as aspirin, warfarin, apixaban, or clopidogrel?
key_questions.looking_for: Use of antithrombotics; may influence management but does not exclude CRAO

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had a stroke or heart attack before age 60?

reasoning_points: Sudden, painless, unilateral severe vision loss
Visual deficit is maximal at onset rather than progressive
Relative afferent pupillary defect in the affected eye
Fundoscopic cherry-red spot with pale edematous retina and narrowed retinal arterioles
No retinal hemorrhages or disc edema and no pain, flashes, or floaters
Vascular risk factors and possible embolic source such as atrial fibrillation or carotid stenosis
Giant cell arteritis must be excluded in patients over 50 with ESR/CRP and relevant symptoms
Managed as a stroke equivalent with urgent vascular and cardiac evaluation

easy: Classic older adult with vascular risk factors
medium: Early presentation before the cherry-red spot is clearly visible
Cilioretinal artery sparing with preserved central acuity
Mildly elevated ESR or CRP in an older adult requiring giant cell arteritis workup
Needs differentiation from non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or vitreous hemorrhage
hard: Young patient with no vascular risk factors and a suspected hypercoagulable state
Concurrent acute cerebral ischemia found on brain MRI
Giant cell arteritis with subtle symptoms and elevated ESR/CRP where steroids must be started immediately
Atypical fundoscopic findings or media opacity limiting the view
